definition: In computer science, online machine learning is a method of machine learning in which data becomes available in a sequential order and is used to update the best predictor for future data at each step, as opposed to batch learning techniques which generate the best predictor by learning on the entire training data set at once.
details: Online learning is a common technique used in areas of machine learning where it is computationally infeasible to train over the entire dataset, requiring the need of out-of-core algorithms. It is also used in situations where it is necessary for the algorithm to dynamically adapt to new patterns in the data, or when the data itself is generated as a function of time, e.g., prediction of prices in the financial international markets. Online learning algorithms may be prone to catastrophic interference, a problem that can be addressed by incremental learning approaches. Online machine learning algorithms find applications in a wide variety of fields such as sponsored search to maximize ad revenue, portfolio optimization, shortest path prediction (with stochastic weights, e.g. traffic on roads for a maps application), spam filtering, real-time fraud detection, dynamic pricing for e-commerce, etc. There is also growing interest in usage of online learning paradigms for LLMs to enable continuous, real-time adaptation after the initial training.

explainer.lead: Online machine learning updates the predictor at each step as data arrives sequentially. It suits cases where training over the whole dataset is infeasible or patterns change over time.

tiers.eli5: It is like learning a game one move at a time and adjusting your strategy after every move.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it when data is too large for in-memory batch training (requiring out-of-core algorithms) or generated as a function of time, such as financial prices. It may be prone to catastrophic interference.
tiers.paperLevel: Data arrives in sequential order and updates the best predictor for future data at each step, unlike batch learning on the entire training set at once. Known limit: prone to catastrophic interference.

explainer.example: Predicting prices in international financial markets, where the data is generated as a function of time.
